relationships.label: Lawyer during CIA planning
relationships.description: Scott identifies Dulles as a Sullivan and Cromwell lawyer when Vandenberg recruited him in 1946 and while he advocated European covert operations; his formal CIA entry came in November 1950.

relationships.label: Director and earlier agency planner
relationships.description: Scott distinguishes Dulles’s pre-agency planning role, formal entry in November 1950 and subsequent service as director, including the 1953 Iran operation.

relationships.label: Established in early summer 1948
relationships.description: Scott explicitly says Dulles set up the American Committee for a United Europe in early summer 1948. This is more specific than the existing association edge.

relationships.label: OSS officer negotiating Italian surrender
relationships.description: Scott describes Dulles as an OSS officer when negotiating with Karl Wolff in 1945, and characterizes his conduct as evading Washington’s restrictions.

relationships.label: Discussed Guatemala policy before directing it
relationships.description: Scott says Dulles discussed overthrow of the Arbenz government in New York at the CFR before orchestrating the policy at CIA; discussion does not alone establish a membership title.

relationships.label: Negotiated conditional German surrender
relationships.description: Scott describes the 1945 negotiations over German forces in Italy and attributes a breach of Roosevelt’s unconditional-surrender understanding to Dulles.

relationships.label: Co-devised covert Marshall Plan provision
relationships.description: Scott names Dulles, Kennan and Forrestal together in devising a secret provision allowing CIA political-warfare funding from reconstruction aid.

relationships.label: Co-devised covert Marshall Plan provision
relationships.description: Scott names Forrestal with Dulles and Kennan in the covert funding arrangement; this is a specific collaborative action, not inferred social affiliation.

relationships.label: Collaborated on covert reconstruction-aid provision
relationships.description: Scott explicitly groups them with Dulles in planning the political-warfare funding provision.

relationships.label: Approved alternative British U-2 authorization arrangement
relationships.description: Scott says Dulles secretly approved a 1957 plan with MI6 to allow the British prime minister to authorize flights rather than depend solely on Eisenhower’s approvals.

relationships.label: Prime-minister authorization role in U-2 arrangement
relationships.description: Macmillan is named as the British prime minister whose authority could be used in the plan; this does not imply that he was an intelligence-service employee.

relationships.label: Senior partner during oil-cartel defense
relationships.description: Scott identifies Foster as senior partner when Arthur Dean resisted the government’s document demand, and notes the later conflict between his State Department role and his former law firm’s representation.

relationships.label: Secretary of state under Eisenhower
relationships.description: Scott identifies the appointment and describes transfer of the oil-cartel antitrust case to State under Dulles.

relationships.label: Represented oil-cartel interests in antitrust dispute
relationships.description: Scott describes the firm’s defense of the oil majors’ cartel agreements. Representation is legal employment, not ownership of the companies.

relationships.label: Oil-company lawyer at the firm
relationships.description: Scott identifies Dean as Exxon’s lawyer at Sullivan and Cromwell and quotes his national-security justification for withholding documents.

relationships.label: Member of six-person CIA advisory group
relationships.description: Scott names Jackson among Dulles’s advisers; Jackson and Wisner subsequently joined CIA.

relationships.label: Head of expanded covert operations program
relationships.description: Scott says Wisner left Wall Street to oversee the enlarged program through the newly created OPC.

relationships.label: AFL official supervising Irving Brown
relationships.description: The paragraph identifies Lovestone as an AFL official and Brown as his assistant.

relationships.label: CIA asset in labor operations
relationships.description: Scott explicitly describes Lovestone as a CIA asset in the account of anti-Communist labor funding.

relationships.label: Acted for CIA-linked labor operation
relationships.description: Scott, citing Valentine, says Ferri-Pisani hired men to attack striking Communist dockworkers on behalf of Brown and CIA. This is an attributed operational claim, not a CIA employment title.

relationships.label: Described as chief Japanese asset
relationships.description: Scott quotes an assessment of Kodama as probably CIA’s chief asset in Japan and discusses his management of M-fund payouts. The article notes that CIA knew about the Lockheed payments but had not admitted involvement.

relationships.label: CIA-cleared U-2 contractor
relationships.description: Scott explicitly identifies Lockheed as the U-2 builder and major CIA-cleared contractor. This does not establish CIA participation in every Lockheed payoff.

relationships.label: Organizer
relationships.description: Scott calls Bernhard the organizer of the Bilderberg Group, rather than merely an associate.

relationships.label: Close friend
relationships.description: Scott explicitly describes Bernhard as a close friend of CIA directors Dulles and Bedell Smith.

relationships.label: Close friend
relationships.description: The friendship is explicitly stated in the Lockheed discussion; it does not demonstrate Smith’s participation in the payments.

relationships.label: CIA director
relationships.description: Scott identifies Smith’s office when describing his friendship with Bernhard.

relationships.label: Long-time supporter
relationships.description: Scott explicitly describes Dasaad as a longstanding supporter of Sukarno before developing ties to Suharto’s circle.

relationships.label: Beneficiary of redirected Indonesian account
relationships.description: Scott names Alamsjah as beneficiary of the new Lockheed account established through Dasaad’s company in May 1965.

relationships.label: Reported plotting allies against Sukarno
relationships.description: Scott says Alamsjah was said to be allied with Sutowo in plotting against Sukarno; the wording is preserved as an attributed report.

relationships.label: Aircraft-deal commission agent
relationships.description: Scott identifies Hasan as commission agent on the agreement to supply 200 Aero-Commander aircraft to the Indonesian Army.

relationships.label: Aircraft supplied under Indonesian Army agreement
relationships.description: The body describes the July 1965 Army delivery agreement; endnote 38 says the aircraft went to the Diponegoro Division.

relationships.label: Co-established shipping companies operated by division
relationships.description: Scott says Hasan and Suharto established two shipping companies to be operated by the Central Java division. The statement is about an operating arrangement, not membership in the division.

relationships.label: Co-established shipping companies operated by division
relationships.description: Scott explicitly ties the jointly established shipping companies to Diponegoro’s operation; the edge does not infer an ownership share or military rank absent from the passage.

relationships.label: Head of army oil company
relationships.description: Scott identifies Sutowo as Permina’s head and discusses the company’s financial role in the operations surrounding Sukarno’s removal.

relationships.label: CIA-controlled proprietary supply firm
relationships.description: Scott describes Sea Supply as proprietary; endnote 89 quotes its CIA-controlled front status and supply of weapons to Nationalist forces in Burma and Thai police.

relationships.label: Supply infrastructure for paramilitary force
relationships.description: Scott explicitly says Sea Supply provided infrastructure for a drug traffic supporting CIA-led PARU; the drug-related characterization remains attributed to Scott.

relationships.label: CIA-led paramilitary force
relationships.description: Scott expressly identifies the force as CIA-led; no independent formal employment or ownership status is implied.

relationships.label: Supplied Nationalist Chinese troops in Burma
relationships.description: Endnote 89 quotes a report that Sea Supply supplied weapons and equipment to 10,000 Nationalist Chinese troops in Burma over almost ten years.

relationships.label: Helped establish and run CIA front
relationships.description: The body says Helliwell set up the company for CIA; endnote 89 dates his involvement to 1951 and says he helped run it.

relationships.label: Helped establish company for CIA
relationships.description: Scott explicitly names CAT, later Air America, among the companies Helliwell established for CIA operations.

relationships.label: Company established for CIA operations
relationships.description: Scott states that Helliwell established CAT for CIA and describes it as infrastructure for covert Southeast Asian operations.

relationships.label: Top adviser with undercover CIA role
relationships.description: Scott says ARAMCO maintained undercover CIA personnel such as Eddy among top advisers until nationalization in 1980; this does not specify Eddy’s individual entire service interval.

relationships.label: Undercover personnel while advising ARAMCO
relationships.description: The undercover CIA description is explicit in Scott’s account and is more specific than a general shared-event link.

relationships.label: Appealed for CIA intervention in Iran; declined
relationships.description: Scott says Truman declined Churchill’s direct personal appeal to involve CIA in overthrowing Mossadeq. This edge preserves the refusal rather than depicting a joint operation.

relationships.label: Dispatched on Tehran negotiating mission
relationships.description: Scott says Truman sent Harriman to seek a peaceful resolution of Mossadeq’s differences with London after declining covert intervention.

relationships.label: Attempted negotiated resolution in Tehran
relationships.description: Scott describes the unsuccessful mission to resolve the Iranian premier’s conflict with Britain; this is a diplomatic transaction, not continuing alliance.

relationships.label: Opposed nationalization through export restrictions
relationships.description: Scott attributes the 1951 boycott of Iranian oil to the majors; endnote 48 records Exxon’s corporate-history denial of conspiracy, so the claim is contested.

relationships.label: Approved TP/AJAX operation against Mossadeq
relationships.description: Scott dates final approval to July 22, 1953, and distinguishes it from earlier oil-company and MI6 efforts.

relationships.label: Member of seven-company oil grouping
relationships.description: Scott includes Anglo-Iranian with five American firms and Royal Dutch Shell in the Seven Sisters. This composition link is distinct from the existing boycott-support edge.

relationships.label: Commercial portfolio divided in 2008 split
relationships.description: Scott describes the original firm dividing into the US-government-focused Booz Allen Hamilton and the commercial/international Booz and Company. This is corporate succession, not a claim of ongoing parent ownership.

relationships.label: Head before entering Booz Allen
relationships.description: Scott traces McConnell’s NSA leadership under Bush and Clinton, his move into Booz Allen, later DNI office and return to the firm.

relationships.label: Executive vice president after government service
relationships.description: The article identifies his executive vice presidency as the end of the described revolving-door sequence. March 2014 is the source vantage, not a historical appointment date.

relationships.label: Accessed NSA records through contractor employment
relationships.description: Scott says Snowden, a Booz Allen employee, departed with NSA records. This edge is contractor access, not a claim that NSA directly employed him.

relationships.label: Employee
relationships.description: Scott explicitly calls Snowden an employee of Booz Allen in discussing the contractor’s media links to NSA.

relationships.label: Contractor relationship illustrated by Snowden access
relationships.description: Scott discusses the private contractor’s NSA connection and the movement of McConnell between NSA and the firm.

relationships.label: Joint overseas mission with Copeland
relationships.description: Scott calls the March 1953 Cairo assignment effectively a joint CIA–Booz Allen mission. The edge does not infer that all overseas assignments mentioned were covert operations.

relationships.label: Employee then on unpaid leave during Khashoggi advisory work
relationships.description: Scott distinguishes his resignation from CIA to join the consultancy from later leave to consult for oil companies and advise Khashoggi.

relationships.label: Advised Nasser on establishing service
relationships.description: Scott explicitly says Copeland advised Nasser on setting up the Mukhabarat; advice is not formal membership or operational control of the service.

relationships.label: Leader advised on establishment
relationships.description: The service was being established for Nasser’s government with Copeland’s advice; the source does not assign a separate founding date here.

relationships.label: Major shareholder and part-owner
relationships.description: Scott explicitly describes Adham’s BCCI shareholding, contrasting it with his intelligence and Khashoggi relationships.

relationships.label: Former principal contact in Arab Middle East
relationships.description: Scott attributes this characterization to the Senate BCCI report; it is a contact role, not an allegation of formal CIA employment.

relationships.label: Selected for covert political-action group
relationships.description: Scott says CIA decided in November 1962 to use Moss for the Political Action Group of its Covert Action staff; the source supplies this operational role independently of Khashoggi’s later public-relations employment.

relationships.label: Chairman in the 1970s
relationships.description: Scott explicitly identifies Moss as chairman of the Kenyan club and describes his invitation to Khashoggi to become majority owner.

relationships.label: Majority owner invited by Moss
relationships.description: The source identifies majority ownership of the property; it explicitly warns against confusing the resort with the intelligence alliance.

relationships.label: Close confidant relationship
relationships.description: Scott identifies Rebozo as Nixon’s close confidant. This personal relationship is separate from disputed stories of money carried to Nixon.

relationships.label: Postwar Vienna counterintelligence chief
relationships.description: Scott identifies Barry as postwar head of OSS Counterintelligence X-2 in Vienna, associated with recovery of SS gold.

relationships.label: Major stockholder
relationships.description: Scott explicitly calls Barry a major stockholder in Rappaport’s Inter Maritime Bank, distinct from a generic banking association.

relationships.label: Personnel held ownership interests
relationships.description: Scott says individuals from Booz Allen formed part of the small ownership group. This is a personnel ownership connection, not a claim that the firm itself owned the company.

relationships.label: Intelligence-service chief
relationships.description: The conventional account quoted by Scott identifies Marenches as chief of the French service.

relationships.label: Reported originator
relationships.description: Scott presents the usual origin story crediting Marenches, then contrasts Mamdani’s account of American official backing. The organizer claim is attributed, not treated as the only account.

relationships.label: Egyptian intelligence component
relationships.description: The alliance is explicitly described as including Egypt’s intelligence service alongside France, Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Iran; this does not make the Kenyan resort that service’s parent.

relationships.label: French intelligence component
relationships.description: Scott explicitly links the French service and its chief to the intelligence alliance; official origins and alleged later circumvention of limits are distinguished.

relationships.label: Dismissed counterintelligence chief in 1974
relationships.description: Scott identifies Colby’s dismissal of Angleton as part of Trento’s account of the later private-network response.

relationships.label: Counterintelligence chief until dismissal
relationships.description: The office and dismissal are explicit in the article; quotation of Angleton’s criticism is not proof of every subsequent private-network allegation.

relationships.label: Reported private-network collaborators
relationships.description: Scott quotes Trento alleging that Helms and Shackley worked with outsiders after Colby’s cooperation with Congress; the account is attributed and contested rather than a documented formal organization chart.

relationships.label: Adviser
relationships.description: Endnote 60 explicitly identifies Bush as a Carlyle adviser. It distinguishes George W. Bush’s Caterair board appointment, which is not transferred to this identity.

relationships.label: Executive committee chairman after CIA service
relationships.description: Scott quotes Phillips that after leaving CIA in January 1977 Bush chaired the executive committee of First International Bancshares and its British subsidiary. This does not identify the subsidiary as BCCI.

relationships.label: Worked closely in intelligence relations
relationships.description: Endnote 100 quotes Phillips on Bush’s close work with Adham, the Saudi intelligence head.

relationships.label: Message proposing meeting routed through Safari Club representative
relationships.description: Scott quotes Mamdani that Rabin’s letter to Sadat passed through the Moroccan representative and helped prepare the 1977 rapprochement.

relationships.label: Partners in early Israeli gun-running
relationships.description: Scott says Greenspun introduced Schwimmer to Khashoggi and describes their earlier gun-running partnership.

relationships.label: Reported collaboration in Israeli gun-running
relationships.description: Endnote 107 cites Slater for collaboration among Greenspun, Schwimmer and Lansky; it separately says Helliwell may have participated, which is not added as a firm edge.

relationships.label: Reported collaboration in Israeli gun-running
relationships.description: The endnote explicitly groups these collaborators; the relationship is attributed to the cited account.

relationships.label: Introduced Khashoggi to Schwimmer
relationships.description: Scott identifies Greenspun’s introduction in Las Vegas as an earlier connection than the 1982 resort meeting.

relationships.label: Collaborated on peace and Iran proposals
relationships.description: Scott describes Kolb’s assistance rewriting the peace plan and joint preparation with Copeland of papers carried by Khashoggi to McFarlane.

relationships.label: Co-prepared paper conveyed by Khashoggi
relationships.description: Kolb and Copeland wrote the strategic proposal and gave it to Khashoggi to present to McFarlane; no direct meeting between Kolb and McFarlane is asserted.

relationships.label: Established contacts and arms-initiative collaboration
relationships.description: Scott describes their earlier introduction by Greenspun, the 1982 meeting and participation in the 1985 Hamburg negotiations. The link is supported by explicit dealings rather than co-occurrence alone.

relationships.label: Met at Kenyan resort in May 1982
relationships.description: Scott explicitly states the meeting of Israeli Defense Minister Sharon with President Nimeiri, alongside Nimrodi, Schwimmer and Kimche.

relationships.label: Participant in May 1982 meeting
relationships.description: Scott names Kimche among the Israelis who met Sudan’s president; no resort ownership or club membership is inferred.

relationships.label: Participant in May 1982 meeting
relationships.description: The explicit meeting description establishes contact, but not a continuing institutional affiliation.

relationships.label: Participant in May 1982 meeting
relationships.description: Scott includes Schwimmer among the Israeli participants in the meeting with Nimeiri.

relationships.label: Board member
relationships.description: Scott identifies Hartmann’s BCCI board position alongside his roles at the other two banks.

relationships.label: Vice-chairman
relationships.description: Scott explicitly identifies Hartmann as vice-chairman of Rappaport’s Swiss bank, distinguishing this office from ownership.

relationships.label: Head of Swiss subsidiary
relationships.description: Scott identifies Hartmann as head of BCCI’s Swiss subsidiary.

relationships.label: Swiss subsidiary
relationships.description: Scott explicitly identifies Banque de Commerce et de Placements as BCCI’s Swiss subsidiary.

relationships.label: Interlocking executive through Hartmann
relationships.description: Hartmann’s simultaneous BCCI board membership and Intermaritime vice-chairmanship establish an executive interlock; the source does not say one bank owned the other.

relationships.label: Co-authored Top Secret America
relationships.description: Scott identifies their joint book and quotes its account of expanding classified government; no agency affiliation is inferred from their research.

profileUpdates.description: Scott describes Booz Allen’s intelligence-contracting work, executive movement between company and government, the 2008 division separating its commercial portfolio, and Copeland’s Cairo mission and later unpaid leave. The article says individual personnel held Paradise Island Bridge ownership interests; it does not say Booz Allen itself owned the company. Carlyle majority ownership is described from the article’s 2014 vantage.

Scott identifies Bush’s Carlyle advisory role and quotes Phillips on his chairmanship of First International Bancshares’ executive committee after leaving CIA. Claims about broader Safari Club and BCCI financing are attributed to Trento; the London-bank wording does not establish a BCCI chairmanship.

Scott describes the Bridge Company as partly owned by a Benguet International officer and by individuals associated with Booz Allen, not the consultancy itself. Alleged transfers to Nixon and Rebozo are distinguished from Scott’s speculative suggestion that Nixon held a hidden interest.

Source describes its political-influence functions and financing, but ambiguous Bush/London wording is not converted into a directorship. Existing financing and CIA-use edges remain attributed.

summary: All 112 existing Scott-source people and organizations reviewed against all 27 PDF pages, including endnotes. Added missing explicit employment, office, ownership, founding, financial, advisory and transaction links and replaced vague associated-with semantics with separately cited specific roles where needed. Source assertions remain attributed; contested memoir and corruption claims retain qualification. No affiliation inferred from being quoted, appearing in the same paragraph, geographical proximity or event attendance alone. Article-publication dates are not used as dates of historical roles. Unknown counterparties and ambiguous institutional identifications are listed for review rather than invented.
